q: Which hormone, made in bigger amounts by men but vital to women's desire too, is a key driver of sex drive?
note: In men, levels usually peak in the morning.

q: Which hormone, also called ADH because it controls urine output, is linked to pair bonding in male mammals?
note: ADH means antidiuretic hormone. Romance and kidney management, one molecule.

q: Which small rodent's loyal, long-term pair bonds made it the poster animal of love-hormone research?
note: Its free-roaming cousin, the meadow vole, has far fewer of the key brain receptors.

q: A 1999 Italian study found people newly in love had serotonin changes resembling those seen in which condition?
note: Lovestruck and obsessive brains both struggle to stop thinking about one thing.

q: Which compound in chocolate was hyped as a 'love chemical', though eating it barely raises levels in the brain?
note: Enzymes destroy most of it before it can get anywhere romantic.

q: Which natural painkillers, named from 'endogenous morphine', are released during sex and exercise?
note: Laughing together releases them too, so a funny partner is a double win.

q: Pounding pulse and sweaty palms when someone you fancy walks in come mostly from which fight-or-flight hormone?
note: Your body basically treats a cute stranger like a charging tiger.

q: A 2005 brain-scan study of intense new love found strong activity in which reward-system region?
note: It sits deep in the midbrain, a hub of the brain's reward circuitry.

q: The reproductive hormone kisspeptin is named after which chocolate, made in the US town where it was discovered?
note: Its gene was found in 1996 in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Sweetest naming story in biology.

q: Anthropologist Helen Fisher split love into three brain systems: lust, attraction and what?
note: Lust wants someone, attraction wants one person, and the last wants them to stay.

q: In Dutton and Aron's 1974 study, men met a woman on a wobbly what, and called her more often?
note: Misattribution of arousal: fear jitters mistaken for chemistry.

q: Liking something more simply because you keep seeing it is called the ___ effect, shown by Zajonc in 1968.
note: Also why that person at the gym slowly gets cuter every week.

q: Which 'P' word do psychologists use for physical nearness as a driver of attraction, famously studied in MIT housing in 1950?
note: Festinger's team found residents mostly befriended the people living closest to them.

q: Arthur Aron's 1997 closeness study had strangers ask each other how many increasingly personal questions?
note: A 2015 New York Times essay made them go viral as a fall-in-love recipe.

q: Robert Sternberg's triangular theory of love has three sides: intimacy, passion and what?
note: Passion alone he called 'infatuated love'; intimacy alone is simply 'liking'.

q: In Sternberg's triangular theory, what is the complete love called, where all three sides are present?
note: Sternberg warned that keeping it can be harder than reaching it.

q: In John Lee's 1973 'colours of love', playful, game-like love is named after which Latin word?
note: Ludus lovers enjoy the chase and often like to keep things light.

q: Which ancient Greek word describes selfless, unconditional love?
note: It's the giving, expect-nothing-back kind of love.

q: Psychologist Dorothy Tennov's 1979 book introduced which word for obsessive, all-consuming infatuation?
note: Replaying one message from them fifty times? Classic symptom.

q: In Hazan and Shaver's 1987 study of adult love styles, the three types were secure, anxious and what?
note: They adapted John Bowlby's theory of early caregiver bonds to grown-up romance.

q: Psychologist Elaine Hatfield contrasted fiery passionate love with which calmer, deeper kind?
note: Passion tends to cool over time; the deeper friendship kind can keep growing.

q: Which of John Gottman's 'horsemen' of relationship doom is the biggest single predictor of divorce?
note: Eye-rolling and sneering are classic signs. His antidote: regular appreciation.

q: Gottman's 'magic ratio' says happy couples have how many positive interactions for each negative one during conflict?
note: Tiffs are fine, as long as affection comfortably outnumbers them.

q: What was the nickname of Gottman's University of Washington research apartment, where couples were observed?
note: Couples spent a weekend there while researchers recorded how they talked and bickered.

q: Gottman calls small attempts to get a partner's attention, like 'Look at that bird!', what?
note: Couples who stayed together responded warmly to these far more often.

q: Research on couples mostly backs which saying about who ends up together?
a: Birds of a feather flock together
options: Absence makes the heart grow fonder
Birds of a feather flock together
note: Similar values, backgrounds and humour predict attraction better than opposites do.

q: In Elliot Aronson's 1966 'pratfall' study, a highly competent person became more likeable after doing what?
note: Tiny blunders make impressive people feel human. Clumsy romantics, rejoice.

q: Claus Wedekind's 1995 'sweaty T-shirt' study linked scent attraction to differences in which group of immune genes?
note: Women tended to prefer the smell of men whose immune genes differed from their own.

q: A 2003 study in Nature found about two-thirds of couples tilt their heads which way when they kiss?
note: The researcher observed couples in public places in the US, Germany and Turkey.

q: The idea that close partners 'sculpt' each other toward their ideal selves is named after which artist?
note: Named for his idea that a statue is freed from a block of marble.

q: A 1972 study claimed parents' disapproval makes couples fall harder. The effect is named after which lovers?
note: A 2014 replication found the opposite: disapproval tends to hurt relationships.

q: What is the fear of falling in love called?
note: Gamophobia, the fear of marriage, is its close cousin.

q: Craving touch after a long time without hugs is nicknamed 'touch starvation' or 'skin ___'?
note: A long hug from someone you trust is the classic fix.

q: Le Petit Robert's 2014 edition finally gave French its own verb for French-kissing. What is it?
note: Until then, French speakers made do with long phrases, or borrowed 'French kiss' itself.

q: Who wrote the 1992 bestseller 'The Five Love Languages'?
note: It has sold millions of copies and been translated into dozens of languages.

q: Your partner washes the dishes and fixes the leaky tap without being asked. Which love language is that?
note: For some people, a scrubbed sink beats a bouquet of flowers.

q: Compliments, 'I'm proud of you' messages and sweet notes speak which love language?
note: A 2024 research review found weak evidence that people have one fixed love language.

q: Which love language is all about undivided attention: phones away, eyes up?
note: A distracted 'mm-hmm' is the fastest way to miss this one.

q: The black, grey, white and purple striped flag, adopted in 2010, represents which orientation?
note: Some in this community wear a black ring on the middle finger as a quiet signal.

q: Which orientation term, from the Greek for 'all', means attraction to people regardless of gender?
note: Its flag has pink, yellow and blue stripes.

q: Someone who experiences little or no romantic attraction, whatever their sexual attraction, identifies as what?
note: Romantic and sexual attraction can run on separate tracks for many people.

q: Which term describes someone who experiences sexual attraction only rarely, or very faintly?
note: Also spelled greysexual; 'gray-A' is a common short form.

q: Someone who finds intelligence the sexiest trait of all might call themselves what?
note: From the Latin 'sapiens', meaning wise. Smart is the new sexy.

q: The pink, purple and blue striped flag, designed by Michael Page in 1998, represents which identity?
note: The purple stripe is where the pink and blue overlap.

q: Monica Helms designed the light blue, pink and white striped flag in 1999 for which community?
note: Helms pointed out it reads correctly whichever way up you fly it.

q: The yellow, white, purple and black striped flag, created by Kye Rowan in 2014, represents which identity?
note: The yellow stripe stands for people whose gender sits outside the binary.

q: The yellow flag with an unbroken purple ring, created in 2013, represents which community?
note: UN estimates put people born with these traits at up to 1.7%.

q: Which term, from the Latin for 'on this side of', describes someone whose gender matches their sex assigned at birth?
note: Chemists use the same prefix for molecules with groups on the same side.

q: Which identity term, adopted at a 1990 gathering in Winnipeg, is used by some Indigenous North American LGBTQ+ people?
note: It's meant for Indigenous people, reflecting their own cultural traditions.

q: What is a person called who isn't LGBTQ+ themselves but actively supports queer rights?
note: There's even a flag: black and white stripes with a rainbow A.

q: Which term, coined by Michael Warner in 1991, describes treating straight relationships as the default?
note: Think every form asking for 'husband's name'.

q: Which term, built from the Latin for 'love', describes assuming everyone wants and needs a romantic relationship?
note: It's why 'Still single?' questions at family weddings can sting.

q: Which US city names the 19th-century term for two independent women living together as life partners?
note: Henry James's novel about such a pair helped popularise the phrase.

q: What was the name of the coded slang used by gay men in mid-20th-century Britain?
note: Words like 'bona' (good) and 'vada' (look) were part of it.

q: National Coming Out Day, first marked in the USA in 1988, falls on which date?
note: The date marks the anniversary of a 1987 LGBT rights march on Washington.

q: In which year did the American Psychiatric Association remove homosexuality from its diagnostic manual, the DSM?
note: It had been listed as a disorder since the manual's first edition.

q: Evelyn Hooker's 1957 study found experts couldn't tell gay and straight men apart using what?
note: Her work helped persuade psychiatry to stop calling homosexuality a disorder.

q: On the original 1978 rainbow flag, what did the hot pink stripe symbolise?
note: Turquoise stood for magic and art; both colours were later dropped.

q: On the six-stripe rainbow flag, which colour was said to stand for healing?
note: Yellow is sunlight, green nature, blue serenity and violet spirit.

q: Who designed the 2018 'Progress' Pride flag, which adds a chevron of extra stripes?
note: The arrow-shaped chevron symbolises forward movement.

q: Which word, blending Greek 'many' and Latin 'love', means having several loving relationships, with everyone's knowledge and agreement?
note: The word is only a few decades old; the practice is far older.

q: What word describes feeling joy when your partner is happy with another partner, the opposite of jealousy?
note: Think of it as being happy that someone you love is being loved.

q: In open-relationship slang, what do you call your partner's other partner?
note: Greek 'meta' plus French 'amour'.

q: What's the popular name for a romantic relationship shared by three people?
note: A blend of 'three' and 'couple'.

q: Which sex columnist coined 'monogamish' for committed couples who allow a little outside fun?
note: His long-running advice column is called 'Savage Love'.

q: Which piece of furniture names the relationship style where all partners, and their partners, can happily share a meal?
note: Its opposite, 'parallel', is when partners barely cross paths.

q: In non-monogamous communities, what does the abbreviation NRE stand for?
note: That giddy, can't-stop-smiling buzz of a brand-new connection.

q: Andie Nordgren's 2006 manifesto argued no relationship should automatically outrank another. What is this style called?
note: Friends, lovers and partners are all valued on their own terms.

q: Which relationship style, nicknamed 'the lifestyle', involves committed couples having sex with others, often together?
note: Swingers' clubs and parties are a major part of that world.

q: Which psychotherapist wrote 'Mating in Captivity' (2006), about keeping desire alive in long relationships?
note: Her argument: desire needs a little distance and mystery to breathe.

q: Emily Nagoski's book 'Come As You Are' explains arousal as a system of accelerators and what?
note: Stress slams the pedal, which is why relaxing can be the best foreplay.

q: Desire that shows up only after things get started, rather than out of the blue, is called what?
note: It's common and completely normal, especially in long-term relationships.

q: Rosemary Basson's 2000 model said many women's desire is better drawn as which shape, not a straight line?
note: Intimacy can spark arousal, which then sparks desire, looping round.

q: What name is given to the warm, satisfied feeling after sex, which a 2017 study found lingers about 48 hours?
note: Couples with a stronger version reported happier relationships months later.

q: Cuddles and sweet chat after sex are sometimes called what, the flip side of foreplay?
note: Don't just roll over and snore. Cuddle responsibly.

q: What's the playful name for sexual activity that doesn't involve penetration?
note: It lowers pregnancy risk, though some STIs still spread through skin contact.

q: The 'Coolidge effect', renewed sexual interest when a new partner appears, is named after which US president?
note: It comes from an old joke about his wife, a busy rooster and many hens.

q: Can someone who is too drunk to understand what's happening give consent?
options: Only if you're in a relationship
note: Consent needs a clear head, freely given, in the moment.

q: Which touch-based couples' exercise, introduced by sex therapists in 1970, deliberately takes orgasm off the table?
note: Removing the pressure to perform often brings the fun back.

q: Which sex therapist added a 'desire' phase to the sexual response cycle in the late 1970s?
note: Her three-phase model ran desire, excitement, orgasm.

q: Which 1976 bestseller, based on surveys of thousands of women, reshaped how people talked about female orgasm?
note: Shere Hite's survey drew over 3,000 responses.

q: Which British doctor co-wrote 'Sexual Inversion' (1897), an early non-judgemental study of homosexuality?
note: He also coined the term 'autoerotism'.

q: Which Indian author wrote 'The World of Homosexuals' (1977), often called India's first serious study of the subject?
note: It ended with a call to decriminalise homosexuality, decades before India did.

q: Which Mumbai gynaecologist answered readers' sex questions in the 'Ask the Sexpert' column well into his 90s?
note: His witty, no-shame replies were celebrated in a 2017 documentary.

q: In John Lee's 'colours of love', which Greek-derived word names practical, sensible, checklist-style love?
note: Compatible careers, values and five-year plans first; fireworks optional.

q: Someone mostly straight but occasionally open to same-sex attraction might describe themselves as what?
note: Psychologist Ritch Savin-Williams wrote a 2017 book about 'mostly straight' men.

q: Which blend word describes a close, affectionate but non-sexual friendship between two men?
note: The 2009 comedy 'I Love You, Man' is a classic of the genre.

q: In dating talk, what does 'DTR' stand for, as in 'we need to have the DTR talk'?
note: Often the most nerve-racking conversation of early dating.

q: Which word, from Old French for 'by love', names an illicit lover?
note: Sounds far classier than 'side piece'.

q: Hand-holding, hugs and a head on your shoulder speak which love language?
note: One 2005 study linked more partner hugs to lower blood pressure in women.

q: What Gen Z term names the flirty period where you're chatting a lot but not officially dating yet?
note: Not dating, not strangers; somewhere in the typing-dots zone.

q: A quick new relationship started soon after a breakup is commonly called a what?
note: Some research suggests they can actually boost confidence after a breakup.

q: What term describes a closed group relationship where members agree to date only within the group?
note: Think of it as an exclusive club, just with more members.

q: Arthur Aron's 2000 study found long-term couples felt more satisfied after doing what together?
note: In one test, couples tackled an obstacle course with their wrists and ankles strapped together.

q: We tend to like people who clearly like us. What do psychologists call this?
note: Knowing someone likes you is one of the strongest nudges toward liking them back.

q: A 2014 study confirmed that faces look more attractive in a group than alone. What is this nicknamed?
note: Barney Stinson named it on How I Met Your Mother years before the science.

q: Psychologist Justin Lehmiller's 2018 book, based on a survey of over 4,000 Americans' sexual fantasies, is titled what?
note: Its main message: most fantasies are far more common than people assume.

q: Which term, popularised by a 2008 psychology book, describes sexual attraction that can shift over time?
note: The author followed a group of women for a decade to track changing attractions.

q: A 2015 study of 168 cultures found romantic lip-kissing was practised in roughly how many of them?
note: It was common in complex societies but rare among many hunter-gatherer groups.

q: Before it meant revealing LGBTQ+ identity, 'coming out' in the early 1900s borrowed from which social event?
note: Gay men joked about 'coming out' into gay society; the 'closet' part was added later.
